newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Patch said to save dieters from death by chocolate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Patch said to save dieters from death by chocolate.

text.p: Just a mouthful of the cake known as "Death by Chocolate" can lead the dieter into a downward, guilty spiral.
Now help is on the way.
With help from a scented, adhesive patch designed to keep people from craving chocolate, dieters will never have to succumb to temptation again.
The Diet Scent patch, from the British firm L.P. Slimline, is based on aromacology studies which say that 95 percent of taste comes from smell.

The small, blue, square patch is saturated with the aroma of a tropical orchid that smells like almond and vanilla, which the manufacturers say "can have an almost immediate effect in diminishing the desire for weight-inducing chocolate, biscuits and cakes" when worn on the hand, wrist or just inside a shirt on the chest.
L.P. Slimline says the patch is completely safe because it works only through the sense of smell and cannot penetrate the skin. It cannot enter the bloodstream or interfere with other medicines.

"It's what we call the Christmas Dinner Syndrome," said Liz Paul, L.P. Slimline's managing director. "Aroused by the cooking smells, all the family are looking forward to the Christmas dinner -- all that is except the cook who has been bending over the stove and whose olfactory senses are saturated.
"By the time the cook has smelt the roasting turkey and steaming pudding for hours, cheese and toast often seem more appetising."

Paul, a restaurant owner who invented the patch, said the idea came to her when she noticed chefs in her restaurant preferred to send out for take-away food rather than eat the dishes they had just prepared. She remembered her mother not wanting to eat the Christmas lunch she had just cooked.
DOCTOR SAYS THEORY MAKES SENSE
Although aromatherapists and doctors will not endorse the patch, they say the theory behind it makes sense.
Dr Alan Hirsch, neurological director of the Smell and Taste Treatment and Research Foundation in Chicago, has just published a book explaining his research linking scent to weight loss.
"It's clear that smelling different odours can help you lose weight," Hirsch said.

After the failure of an early test in which medical students were asked to sniff a chocolate bar whenever they craved chocolate -- the students ate the chocolate -- Hirsch said he revamped his study and trapped certain odours in a test tube instead.
The first study "only proved two things," he said. "You can't trust medical students and they were acting on the Pavlovian response (of smelling the food and immediately wanting to eat it)."

Because the test tubes could not be eaten, he said the test was able to move beyond initial eating instincts. He tested people for six months with peppermint, green apple and banana smells and found an average weight loss of 30 lbs (14 kg) for those who had a normal sense of smell.

Though Hirsch said it is not clear whether the scents triggered a physiological change that tricked the body into thinking it had just eaten the food or whether it was just reconditioning of the Pavlovian response, he did note that the tests seemed to imply that the more the person liked the smell that more weight loss occurred.
In fact, Hirsch said he had to stop the experiment because subjects were losing too much weight and becoming underweight.

But he emphasised that his study covered only three scents over six months. After the six months, "we don't know what happened to the people, and we don't know if this works for all odours." He is currently working on another test over 13 months.

Aromatherapist Geraldine Howard said the theory behind the patch made sense "because it's perfectly true that some smells can affect the limbic system and cause a physiological response in the body. But I would still view (Diet Scent) with severe scepticism."
Howard said "in all our reference books, there has been no reference in any of them for that oil to be used for that particular purpose" of deadening chocolate cravings.
But for those desperate to be masters of their chocolate cravings, the patch can only be obtained through mail order.
In Britain, Paul said the company was in talks with UniChem, AAH and Boots pharmacies to carry the patches by June.
Or, as Hirsch says, "you can just buy a chocolate bar, throw the chocolate bar away and sniff the wrapper whenever you get a craving."
